curriculum.lesson_evidence: A dance relationship is how one body relates to another body or to an imagined partner. Beside means sharing a side, with similar facing and a gap so elbows do not collide. Mirroring means matching the action on the opposite side, like a reflection. Contrast means a clear difference, such as one dancer still while the other travels. A real partner is optional. A solo dancer can name where the imagined partner stands and still show their own side of the relationship.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Describe a four-count relationship study that uses beside, then mirroring, then contrast. A real partner is optional. If you work alone, how will a viewer still understand the missing partner?

FEEDBACK
Stand beside with a clear gap, mirror one opposite arm, then contrast by freezing one side. A solo plan names where the imagined partner stands and which action they would do. The relationship is the match or the difference, not merely being in a room with someone. Words plus a simple map are enough.

WATCH FOR
Relationships cannot be learned without a real partner standing in the room with you today. Relationship is a choice you can plan and describe. Naming beside, mirroring or contrast, and showing your own side, is real dance evidence. No one is required to partner if they need more space.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Plan a four-count goodbye study that uses beside, mirroring and contrast with either a real or an imagined partner. Keep a gap for personal space, and do not copy the window study. State which side you would do if you are working alone.

Write a short reflection naming one artistic choice you changed and why. Movement or instrument work is optional, adult-supervised and can be described instead.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Kai stands beside Ren, both facing a window, with a gap so their elbows never meet. When they mirror, Kai lifts the right arm and Ren lifts the left arm together. For contrast, Kai sinks and stays still while Ren walks a slow curve. If Ren is away, Kai writes "imagined partner on my left" and leaves a visible gap, performing only Kai's side.

TRY FIRST
Describe a four-count relationship study that uses beside, then mirroring, then contrast. A real partner is optional. If you work alone, how will a viewer still understand the missing partner?

FEEDBACK
Stand beside with a clear gap, mirror one opposite arm, then contrast by freezing one side. A solo plan names where the imagined partner stands and which action they would do. teaching.feedback: The new example should use the same arts idea as the model, but with different content or material.
teaching.fix: Name the element or technique and its effect, not just decoration.
teaching.guided_attempt: Make or describe one fresh example that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your main choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new artwork or performance.
teaching.model: A dance relationship is how one body relates to another body or to an imagined partner. Beside means sharing a side, with similar facing and a gap so elbows do not collide. Mirroring means matching the action on the opposite side, like a reflection. Contrast means a clear difference, such as one dancer still while the other travels. A real partner is optional. A solo dancer can name where the imagined partner stands and still show their own side of the relationship. Now choose a different subject or piece to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same arts idea in a new artwork, song, drama or dance, not a copy of the example. Review clarity, safety and respectful practice.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make intentional visual, music, drama or dance choices and name their effect, rather than saying an artwork is simply “nice”. Keep every claim linked to an element or technique.

visuals.alt: Two panels contrast requiring a live partner with naming an imagined partner and dancing one side.
visuals.teaches: Beside, mirror and contrast can be planned with a partner or described as a solo with an imagined partner.

visuals.alt: Two panels show beside as matched facing with a gap, then mirror arms and a contrast where one dancer is still.
visuals.teaches: Beside shares a side with space between bodies. Mirror matches opposite sides. Contrast makes a clear difference.
